authored_against: Grade 4 science, elementary band. Keys state established science at this grade band; they are not extracted from the source, which states only a focus and generic objectives.

relationships: An observation is information taken in directly, through the senses or through an instrument.
An inference goes beyond the observation to say what it might mean, and the same observation can support more than one inference.
Observations recorded as they are made are more trustworthy than ones written up from memory afterwards.
accepted_alternative_framings: Qualitative and quantitative, or words and numbers, are both correct ways to sort observations.
disqualifying_errors: Recording an inference as an observation, such as 'the circuit is broken' instead of 'the bulb did not light'.
Treating an opinion about what happened as data.
Claiming an observation is only valid if an instrument was used.
topics.out_of_scope: Measurement uncertainty, calibration, and statistical treatment of repeats are later grades and must not be required here.

relationships: A testable question can be answered by making observations or by doing something and seeing what happens.
A testable question names what will be changed or examined and what will be observed or measured.
A question that no possible observation could settle is not testable, however interesting it is.
accepted_alternative_framings: Comparison questions, cause questions, and 'what happens if' questions are all testable forms.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a question testable when no observation could answer it.
Claiming a question has to start with 'why' to count as scientific.
Confusing a question that is looked up in a source with one the learner tested.
topics.out_of_scope: Naming independent and dependent variables formally, and writing hypotheses in if-then form, are later work.

relationships: A model or diagram represents something in order to explain or predict how it behaves.
Every model simplifies, and what it leaves out is a limitation to be stated rather than hidden.
A diagram's labels and arrows carry meaning; an unlabelled diagram does not communicate a model.
accepted_alternative_framings: A labelled drawing, a flow diagram, a physical build, and an acted sequence are all legitimate models here.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a model has to look like the real thing to be good.
Claiming a good model has no limitations.
Judging a diagram on neatness rather than on what it explains.
topics.out_of_scope: Mathematical and computational modelling is later work.

fixed_facts: In a fair test only one thing is changed on purpose; everything else that could affect the result is held the same.
relationships: In a fair test one thing is changed on purpose and everything else that could affect the result is held the same.
If two things change at once, the result cannot be attributed to either one.
Repeating a test and getting a similar result gives more confidence than a single trial does.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a test fair when more than one condition was changed.
Treating one trial as proof.
Treating a result that disagrees with the prediction as a failed test rather than as evidence.
topics.out_of_scope: Control groups by name, randomisation, and sample-size reasoning are later work.

fixed_facts: A measurement is incomplete without its unit.
relationships: A measurement has a number and a unit, and both are needed for it to mean anything.
Repeated measurements of the same quantity usually differ a little; that spread is information about the method, not a mistake to hide.
A labelled table lets values be compared; scattered notes usually do not.
accepted_alternative_framings: Metric or customary units are both acceptable if one system is used consistently within a comparison.
disqualifying_errors: Recording a number with no unit and calling the measurement complete.
Altering a recorded value so it agrees with a prediction or with another trial.
Claiming more decimal places automatically means a better measurement.
topics.out_of_scope: Significant figures, uncertainty ranges, and error propagation are later work.

relationships: Criteria are what a successful solution has to achieve; constraints are the limits it has to work within, including materials, cost, time, and safety.
Criteria and constraints are stated before solutions are generated, so every solution is judged the same way.
A solution that breaks a constraint has not solved the problem, however well it meets the criteria.
disqualifying_errors: Treating criteria and constraints as the same thing.
Declaring a design best without stating what it was judged against.
Adding or dropping a criterion after testing so a preferred design wins.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted trade-off matrices and formal optimisation are later work.

fixed_facts: A moving object has energy of motion; a faster-moving object of the same mass has more of it.
relationships: Any moving object has energy because of its motion.
For objects of the same mass, the faster one has more energy of motion.
For objects moving at the same speed, the more massive one has more energy of motion.
accepted_alternative_framings: 'Energy of motion' and 'kinetic energy' are the same idea; either name is correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a moving object has no energy until it hits something.
Claiming energy of motion depends on speed alone, with mass making no difference.
Claiming an object stores up force as it moves.
topics.out_of_scope: The relationship that energy of motion goes with the square of the speed, and any energy formula, are later work; a learner who states it correctly is not wrong.

relationships: Speed describes how far an object travels in a given time.
Increasing an object's speed increases its energy of motion.
Energy has to be transferred to an object to speed it up, and away from it to slow it down.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing speed in words, as a distance per time, or by comparison between two objects are all acceptable at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an object speeds up or slows down without any energy transfer.
Claiming that speed and energy are the same quantity.
Comparing speeds measured over different distances or times without saying so.
topics.out_of_scope: Calculating speed as distance divided by time is acceptable but not required; acceleration is later work.

relationships: An explanation says how or why something happens; evidence is the recorded observation or measurement that supports it.
An explanation is only as strong as the evidence tied to it.
Evidence that does not bear on the claim does not support it, however carefully it was collected.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a claim with no evidence and calling it an explanation.
Offering evidence that does not bear on the claim being made.
Treating a confident statement as though it were evidence.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal claim-evidence-reasoning terminology and rebuttal structure are later work.

fixed_facts: In a collision, energy is transferred between the colliding objects and into sound, heat, and deformation.
relationships: When objects collide, energy is transferred from one object to the other.
Some of the energy in a collision is transferred to sound, to warming, and to changing the shape of the objects.
A faster collision transfers more energy, which is why faster collisions do more damage.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy disappears in a collision.
Claiming a collision creates new energy.
Claiming the heavier object always transfers energy and never receives any.
topics.out_of_scope: Momentum, elastic versus inelastic collisions, and conservation calculations are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: A prediction about a collision or a motion is based on a pattern established by earlier observation.
A prediction is stated before the test; a statement made afterwards is an explanation.
A prediction that turns out wrong is useful evidence and is recorded exactly as it was made.
disqualifying_errors: Changing a recorded prediction after seeing the result.
Predicting for conditions the observed pattern never covered.
Claiming a prediction is certain rather than expected.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative prediction from equations is later work.

relationships: A scientific question about energy names what would be changed and what would be observed or measured.
Good questions often come from something that does not fit an existing explanation.
A question that cannot be answered by any observation is not a scientific question, whatever else it is.
disqualifying_errors: Framing a preference or a value judgement as a scientific question.
Asking a question with no observable outcome and calling it testable.
Claiming a question is unscientific merely because it is simple.
topics.out_of_scope: Operational definitions and formal variable naming are later work.

fixed_facts: Sound is produced by vibrating matter and needs matter to travel through.
relationships: Sound is produced when matter vibrates, and the vibration passes through the material around it.
Sound travels through solids, liquids, and gases; it cannot travel through empty space.
A larger vibration carries more energy and is heard as a louder sound.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing sound as a vibration passing through matter, or as a wave in matter, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming sound travels through a vacuum.
Claiming sound is made without anything vibrating.
Claiming loudness comes from how fast the sound travels.
topics.out_of_scope: Frequency and pitch as a formal relationship, the speed of sound in named materials, and wave equations are later work.

fixed_facts: Light travels from a source, and it travels in straight lines until something changes its path.
relationships: Light carries energy away from a source such as the Sun, a flame, or a lamp.
Light travels in straight lines until it is reflected, absorbed, or bent by a material.
Light that is absorbed by a material transfers energy to it, which is why dark surfaces in sunlight warm up.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing light as rays or as beams are both acceptable representations at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming light comes out of the eye to make objects visible.
Claiming light bends around ordinary opaque objects so you can see behind them.
Claiming a mirror creates light rather than reflecting it.
topics.out_of_scope: The wave and particle models of light, the speed of light, and the electromagnetic spectrum are later work.

fixed_facts: Energy moves from the warmer object to the cooler one, never the other way on its own.
relationships: When two objects at different temperatures touch, energy moves from the warmer one to the cooler one.
Transfer continues until the two objects reach the same temperature.
Some materials transfer energy quickly and others slowly, which is what makes insulators useful.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying energy is transferred, or that heat flows, are both acceptable at this grade provided the direction is right.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming cold moves into a warm object; only energy moves, and it moves from warmer to cooler.
Claiming an insulator produces warmth rather than slowing transfer.
Claiming a material feels colder because it is at a lower temperature than the air around it, when it is the rate of transfer that differs.
topics.out_of_scope: Conduction, convection, and radiation as named mechanisms, and specific heat capacity, are Grade 7 and later work.

fixed_facts: An electric current needs a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal of the source back to the other.
relationships: Energy can be transferred from place to place by electric currents.
A current flows only in a complete circuit; a break anywhere stops it everywhere in that loop.
A device in a circuit converts the energy delivered to it into another form, such as light, sound, motion, or warmth.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing the circuit as a loop, a path, or a closed circuit are all correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a bulb lights with a wire on only one terminal of the battery.
Claiming a battery stores current rather than storing energy.
Claiming current is used up as it goes round the circuit so less returns to the battery.
topics.out_of_scope: Voltage, resistance, series and parallel analysis, and Ohm's law are later work.

relationships: Energy transfer is observed through its effects: something moves, warms, lights up, makes sound, or changes shape.
Observing an effect is evidence that energy was transferred, not a direct sight of the energy itself.
The same transfer can often be detected by more than one effect, and agreement between them strengthens the evidence.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming energy itself was seen or held.
Claiming no transfer happened because no effect was looked for.
Treating a single ambiguous effect as proof of a particular transfer path.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantifying energy transferred, and efficiency calculations, are later work.

relationships: Energy can be traced from a source, through transfers, to where it ends up.
At every step some energy is transferred to the surroundings, usually as warming, and that step belongs in the trace.
A complete trace names the source, each transfer, and the final form.
accepted_alternative_framings: An arrow diagram, a labelled sequence, or a written account are all valid ways to show the path.
disqualifying_errors: Showing energy appearing partway along the path with no source.
Showing energy vanishing at the end of the path rather than being transferred to the surroundings.
Claiming a device creates the energy it delivers.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative energy accounting and named efficiency figures are later work.

fixed_facts: Energy is not created or destroyed by a device; it is converted from one form to another.
relationships: A device converts energy from one form to another, such as electrical to light, or motion to sound.
No device converts all the energy it receives into the form that is wanted; some always ends up warming the surroundings.
The energy a device delivers comes from a source, never from the device itself.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying energy is converted, transformed, or changed in form are all correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a device creates energy.
Claiming a device converts all of its input into the useful output.
Claiming energy is destroyed when a device stops working.
topics.out_of_scope: Numerical efficiency, the conservation law stated formally, and the second law are later work.

relationships: Design criteria state what the converter has to achieve, in terms that can actually be checked.
A criterion that cannot be tested cannot be used to judge the design.
Safety limits are constraints, and they are not traded away for better performance.
disqualifying_errors: Writing a criterion so vague that no test could settle whether it was met.
Treating a safety limit as negotiable.
Judging the design against criteria written after the test.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal requirements specification and engineering standards are later work.

relationships: More than one design can meet the same criteria, and generating several before choosing gives a better chance of a good one.
Comparing alternatives is only meaningful when they are judged against the same criteria.
An idea that fails a constraint is eliminated at this stage, not tested and then rejected.
disqualifying_errors: Committing to the first idea and calling the comparison done.
Comparing two designs against different criteria.
Keeping a design that breaks a stated constraint because it performs well otherwise.
topics.out_of_scope: Structured ideation methods and decision matrices are later work.

relationships: A build follows the design, and any departure from the design is recorded as it happens.
The device that is tested is the device that was built, not the one that was drawn.
A build that cannot be described well enough for someone else to repeat it cannot be evaluated properly.
disqualifying_errors: Reporting the intended design rather than what was actually built.
Leaving out a change made during the build that affected the result.
Claiming a result for a device that was never completed.
topics.out_of_scope: Tolerances, materials specification, and formal build documentation are later work.

relationships: A test changes one thing at a time so an improvement can be attributed to a particular change.
A failed test is evidence about the design and is the normal route to a better one.
Refinement is judged against the original criteria, not against how much effort the change took.
disqualifying_errors: Changing several things between tests and crediting the improvement to one of them.
Discarding a test result because it was disappointing.
Declaring the design improved without retesting it against the criteria.
topics.out_of_scope: Statistical comparison of design variants is later work.

relationships: Designs are compared against the same criteria and constraints, using the same test.
A design can win on one criterion and lose on another, and an honest comparison reports both.
The comparison reports what the tests showed, not what the designer hoped.
disqualifying_errors: Naming a winner without saying what the criteria were.
Testing two designs under different conditions and comparing the results.
Omitting a criterion on which the preferred design performed badly.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted scoring and formal trade studies are later work.

fixed_facts: A wave transfers energy from place to place without transporting the material it travels through.
relationships: Waves are regular repeating patterns of motion that transfer energy from one place to another.
The material a wave travels through moves back and forth about its resting position; it is not carried along with the wave.
Waves can be described by their amplitude and their wavelength.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing a wave by a diagram, by a demonstration with a rope or spring, or in words are all acceptable.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a wave carries the water or the rope along with it.
Claiming a wave transfers matter rather than energy.
Claiming a single pulse with no repetition shows a wavelength.
topics.out_of_scope: The frequency-wavelength-speed relationship, and wave equations, are Grade 8 and High School work.

fixed_facts: Amplitude is the height of a wave from its resting position, and a larger amplitude carries more energy.
relationships: Amplitude is measured from the resting position to the crest, not from trough to crest.
A wave with larger amplitude carries more energy than an otherwise identical wave with smaller amplitude.
In sound, larger amplitude is heard as louder; in water, larger amplitude is a taller wave.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing amplitude as wave height above rest, or as how far the material moves from rest, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Confusing amplitude with wavelength.
Claiming amplitude sets the pitch of a sound.
Measuring amplitude from trough to crest and reporting it as the amplitude.
topics.out_of_scope: The relationship between energy and the square of the amplitude is later work.

fixed_facts: Wavelength is the distance from one point on a wave to the matching point on the next wave, such as crest to crest.
relationships: Wavelength is the distance from a point on one wave to the matching point on the next.
Wavelength and amplitude are independent: changing one does not force the other to change.
Wavelength is a distance and is reported with a length unit.
accepted_alternative_framings: Crest-to-crest and trough-to-trough both give the wavelength.
disqualifying_errors: Confusing wavelength with amplitude.
Reporting a wavelength with no length unit.
Claiming a taller wave must have a longer wavelength.
topics.out_of_scope: Frequency, period, and the wave speed relationship are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: A wave can make an object in its path move, because it transfers energy to that object.
An object floating on water bobs up and down as waves pass; it is not carried along by them.
A wave with more energy makes a larger motion in the object it reaches.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a floating object is carried forward by each passing wave.
Claiming a wave moves an object without transferring energy to it.
Claiming the object's motion is unrelated to the wave's amplitude.
topics.out_of_scope: Wave-particle interaction models and orbital water motion are later work.

relationships: Patterns can be used to send information: a code of light flashes, sounds, or marks stands for something the sender and receiver agree on.
Information is carried by the pattern, not by the material; the same message can be sent as light, sound, or writing.
A receiver can only recover the message if it knows the code the sender used.
accepted_alternative_framings: Morse code, flag signals, drumbeats, and binary patterns are all correct examples.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming information travels without any physical carrier.
Claiming a pattern carries meaning on its own, without an agreed code.
Claiming a message cannot be converted from one carrier to another.
topics.out_of_scope: Digital versus analog encoding, bandwidth, and error correction are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Communication solutions are compared on how reliably, how far, and how quickly they carry the message, and on what they cost or require.
A solution that works well in one setting can fail in another, so the setting is part of the comparison.
The comparison uses the same criteria for every option.
disqualifying_errors: Declaring one method best without naming the criteria or the setting.
Ignoring a failure mode because it did not appear in the one test run.
Comparing options that were tested under different conditions.
topics.out_of_scope: Signal-to-noise reasoning and quantitative reliability are later work.

fixed_facts: An object is seen when light reflected from it enters the eye.
relationships: Light bounces off surfaces, and that bouncing is reflection.
A smooth surface reflects light in a regular way and gives an image; a rough surface scatters it in many directions and does not.
An object that gives out no light of its own is seen only because light from a source reflects off it.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying light bounces, reflects, or is scattered are all acceptable at this grade provided the direction of travel is right.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the eye sends out light to see objects.
Claiming a non-luminous object can be seen in complete darkness.
Claiming a mirror makes its own light.
topics.out_of_scope: The law of reflection stated with angles, refraction, and image formation are later work.

fixed_facts: Seeing requires light travelling from a source, reflecting off the object, and entering the eye.
relationships: Light from a source reflects off an object, enters the eye, and is detected there.
The eye detects the light; the brain interprets the signal as an image.
Without light entering the eye, nothing is seen, however close or large the object is.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming vision works by the eye reaching out to the object.
Claiming an object is visible in a completely dark room once the eyes adjust.
Claiming the eye forms the perception without the brain.
topics.out_of_scope: Lens optics, the retina and its cell types, and colour vision mechanisms are later work.

relationships: Light paths are modelled with straight arrows that start at the source and point in the direction the light travels.
A complete model of seeing shows the path source, object, eye, in that order.
The arrows are a model of the path; they are not something visible in the room.
accepted_alternative_framings: Ray diagrams drawn with lines or with arrows are both acceptable, provided direction is shown.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing arrows from the eye to the object.
Drawing light travelling in curves around an obstacle.
Omitting the source from the path and starting at the object.
topics.out_of_scope: Scale ray diagrams, angles of incidence and reflection, and lens ray tracing are later work.

relationships: Animals take in information about their surroundings through sense receptors: eyes, ears, skin, nose, and tongue.
Each kind of receptor responds to a particular kind of input, such as light, sound, pressure, or chemicals.
The information is sent from the receptor to the brain as signals.
accepted_alternative_framings: Naming the sense organ or the kind of input it responds to are both acceptable ways to answer here.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming one receptor responds equally to every kind of input.
Claiming the sense organ decides what to do without the brain.
Claiming an animal responds to information it has no receptor for.
topics.out_of_scope: Neurons, synapses, and signal transduction are Grade 7 and High School work.

relationships: Information from the senses is processed in the brain, which is what leads to a response.
A response can be immediate action, or storing the information as memory for later.
Different animals respond differently to the same information, because their bodies and behaviours differ.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the response happens in the sense organ with no processing.
Claiming memory is stored in the sense organ.
Claiming every animal must respond identically to the same input.
topics.out_of_scope: Named brain regions, reflex arcs, and neurotransmission are later work.

relationships: A model of information processing shows input, processing, and response as distinct stages.
The model shows the direction of flow, from receptor to brain to response.
A model that omits the processing stage cannot explain why responses differ between animals or situations.
accepted_alternative_framings: Flow diagrams, labelled drawings, and written sequences are all acceptable model forms.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing a model that runs from response back to input as the normal direction.
Leaving out the processing stage and calling the model complete.
Claiming the model shows what actually happens inside the brain in detail.
topics.out_of_scope: Neural circuitry and computational models of cognition are later work.

relationships: Plants and animals have external structures, such as leaves, thorns, fur, claws, shells, and scales, that support survival, growth, behaviour, and reproduction.
A structure supports survival by doing something specific: protecting, capturing, moving, sensing, or attracting.
The same kind of structure can serve different functions in different organisms.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a structure exists because the organism wanted or needed it.
Naming a structure without saying what it does for the organism.
Claiming every external structure has exactly one function.
topics.out_of_scope: Evolutionary explanation of how structures arose is Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Internal structures such as bones, hearts, lungs, stomachs, roots, and stems support survival, growth, behaviour, and reproduction.
Internal and external structures work together; neither functions alone.
An internal structure's function can be inferred from where it is and what it connects to, and then checked against evidence.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming internal structures matter only to animals and not to plants.
Claiming a structure has a function without any evidence for it.
Claiming internal structures work independently of the rest of the organism.
topics.out_of_scope: Cells, tissues, and organ systems as a hierarchy are Grade 7 and High School work.

relationships: A structure's shape and material relate to what it does; this is the structure-function relationship.
Changing the structure changes what it can do.
Similar functions in different organisms are often carried out by structures that are built differently.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming structure and function are unrelated.
Claiming organisms with the same function must have the same structure.
Claiming a structure changes during an organism's life to fit a new function it needs.
topics.out_of_scope: Adaptation as an evolutionary process, and convergent evolution, are later work.

fixed_facts: Roots take in water and dissolved minerals; leaves are where the plant makes its food.
relationships: Roots anchor the plant and take in water and dissolved minerals from the soil.
Stems support the plant and carry water and food between roots and leaves.
Leaves are where the plant makes its own food, using light.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying leaves make food using light from the Sun, or that they carry out photosynthesis, are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming plants take in ready-made food from the soil.
Claiming roots make the plant's food.
Claiming a plant does not need light if it has enough water and soil.
topics.out_of_scope: The chemistry of photosynthesis, xylem and phloem by name, and gas exchange detail are Grade 7 and High School work.

relationships: Animal structures support taking in food and water, moving, sensing, protecting, and reproducing.
A structure that supports one function often constrains another, such as heavy armour limiting speed.
Structures that look alike can serve different functions in different animals, and structures that look different can serve the same one.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a structure is present for no function at all without evidence.
Claiming an animal grew a structure because it needed one.
Claiming structures never involve trade-offs.
topics.out_of_scope: Homology, analogy, and evolutionary relationship are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: An argument about structure and function states a claim, cites observed evidence, and explains how the evidence supports the claim.
Evidence for a function comes from observing the structure being used, or from its position, shape, and connections.
An argument covers only what the evidence reaches, and says where it stops.
disqualifying_errors: Asserting a function with no evidence and no reasoning.
Using evidence about one organism to make a claim about all organisms.
Treating a plausible story as evidence.
topics.out_of_scope: Counter-argument structure and formal rebuttal are later work.

fixed_facts: In undisturbed sedimentary layers, a lower layer formed before the layer above it.
relationships: Sedimentary rock forms as sediment settles in layers, with newer material on top.
In an undisturbed sequence, deeper means older.
Layers can be tilted, folded, faulted, or eroded after they form, so a sequence has to be checked for disturbance before the rule is applied.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the topmost layer is the oldest.
Reading an age in years straight off the layer order.
Applying the deeper-is-older rule to visibly overturned layers without saying so.
topics.out_of_scope: Radiometric dating, formal stratigraphic principles by name, and correlation between regions are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Fossils in rock layers are evidence of the organisms that lived when those layers were forming.
Different layers often contain different fossils, which is evidence that the living things in a place changed over time.
Fossils of organisms that lived in water, found in layers now far from water, are evidence that the environment there has changed.
disqualifying_errors: Dating a fossil by when it was collected rather than by the layer it came from.
Claiming absence of a fossil proves the organism never lived there.
Claiming the environment at a place has always been what it is today.
topics.out_of_scope: Index fossils, biostratigraphy, and absolute dating are later work.

fixed_facts: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion moves the pieces away.
relationships: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces where it sits, by water, ice, wind, temperature change, plants, and chemical action.
Water freezing in a crack expands and widens the crack, which is why freeze-thaw is a powerful weathering process in Michigan.
Weathering and erosion are different processes: weathering breaks material down, erosion carries it away.
accepted_alternative_framings: Physical and chemical weathering, or mechanical and chemical weathering, are both correct namings.
disqualifying_errors: Using weathering and erosion as though they meant the same thing.
Claiming water contracts when it freezes.
Claiming weathering only happens to rock that is exposed at the surface of a cliff.
topics.out_of_scope: Named chemical weathering reactions and mineral stability series are later work.

relationships: The rate of erosion depends on the slope, the amount and speed of moving water or wind, the material, and whether plants hold it in place.
Faster-moving water carries more material and larger pieces than slower-moving water.
Plant roots slow erosion by holding soil together, which is why removing vegetation increases it.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming erosion happens at the same rate everywhere regardless of slope or cover.
Claiming slow-moving water carries larger material than fast-moving water.
Claiming erosion only happens during storms.
topics.out_of_scope: Sediment transport equations and quantitative erosion rates are later work.

relationships: Maps show where Earth's features are, and patterns in those locations are evidence about the processes that made them.
A map needs a key and a scale, or its symbols and distances cannot be read.
Features such as mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes are not spread evenly over Earth; they cluster in patterns.
accepted_alternative_framings: Topographic maps, relief maps, and thematic maps are all legitimate map types here.
disqualifying_errors: Reading distances off a map with no scale.
Claiming Earth's major features are spread evenly across the surface.
Treating a map symbol as the feature itself rather than as a representation of it.
topics.out_of_scope: Plate tectonics as the explanation for the patterns is Grade 8 and High School work.

fixed_facts: The Great Lakes basins were shaped by continental glaciers during the most recent ice age.
relationships: Michigan's landscape was shaped by continental ice sheets that advanced and retreated repeatedly, carving basins and leaving behind sand, gravel, and boulders.
Much of Michigan's bedrock is sedimentary rock formed in ancient shallow seas, which is why marine fossils such as corals are found there.
Michigan's shorelines and dunes are still being changed today by waves, currents, wind, and ice.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying glaciers, ice sheets, or continental ice all correctly name the agent that shaped the Great Lakes basins.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the Great Lakes were formed by volcanic eruptions or by meteorite impact.
Claiming Michigan's landscape has not changed since the ice retreated.
Claiming fossil corals in Michigan rock mean corals live there in the lakes now.
topics.out_of_scope: Glacial stratigraphy, isostatic rebound, and the Michigan Basin's formation history are later work.

fixed_facts: Renewable resources are replenished on a human timescale; fossil fuels are not.
relationships: The energy people use comes from natural resources: sunlight, wind, moving water, biomass, fossil fuels, and nuclear fuels.
Renewable resources are replaced on a human timescale; fossil fuels form over many millions of years and are not.
Every energy resource has to be found, extracted or captured, converted, and delivered, and each of those steps has costs and effects.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming any energy resource has no environmental effect at all.
Claiming fossil fuels are renewable because they are still forming.
Claiming energy is created at a power plant rather than converted there.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative energy budgets, capacity factors, and life-cycle analysis are later work.

fixed_facts: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
relationships: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other substances into the air.
Extracting, transporting, and burning fuels affects land, water, and air, and those effects differ between fuels.
Reducing the amount of fuel used reduces the effects, which is why efficiency and conservation matter.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming burning fuel produces no waste products because the flame looks clean.
Claiming all fuels have identical environmental effects.
Claiming an effect can be removed entirely rather than reduced.
topics.out_of_scope: The greenhouse mechanism, combustion chemistry, and emissions figures are Grade 7 and later work.

relationships: Natural Earth processes such as floods, storms, erosion, and, elsewhere, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, happen whether or not people are present.
These processes become hazards when they affect people and what they depend on.
Where and when many of these processes occur follows patterns that can be studied and used for planning.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming natural Earth processes can be stopped from happening.
Claiming these processes occur completely at random with no patterns at all.
Claiming Michigan is at risk from active volcanoes.
topics.out_of_scope: Probabilistic hazard assessment and return periods are later work.

relationships: The impact of a natural hazard can be reduced by design, by warning systems, and by where and how people build.
Reducing impact is not the same as preventing the event; the event still happens.
Every mitigation has costs and limits, and a solution that works for one hazard may not work for another.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a design prevents the natural event itself.
Claiming a mitigation removes all risk.
Proposing a mitigation with no reference to the hazard it addresses.
topics.out_of_scope: Engineering codes, cost-benefit analysis, and risk quantification are later work.

relationships: Solutions are compared against the same criteria and constraints, including cost, safety, and who is affected.
A solution can be better on one criterion and worse on another, and the comparison says so.
The comparison is based on tested evidence, not on preference.
disqualifying_errors: Naming a best solution with no criteria stated.
Comparing solutions evaluated under different conditions.
Leaving out a criterion the preferred solution fails.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted decision matrices and formal trade studies are later work.

relationships: Where people in Michigan live and work is shaped by the Great Lakes, by farmland and forests, and by mineral and energy resources.
Michigan's main weather-related hazards include severe thunderstorms, tornadoes, winter and lake-effect snow storms, flooding, and shoreline erosion.
Decisions about resources and hazards affect different communities differently, so who is affected is part of the evidence.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming Michigan faces significant volcanic or major earthquake hazard.
Claiming a resource decision affects every community in the same way.
Claiming the Great Lakes have no effect on Michigan's weather.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal environmental justice frameworks and policy analysis are Grade 8 and later work.
